name: Homomorphic Encryption
description: Homomorphic encryption lets a server compute on data that stays encrypted, so the server never sees the underlying values. The data owner encrypts the inputs, the server performs the arithmetic directly on the encrypted data, and only the holder of the secret key can decrypt the result. For machine learning, the model is first rewritten using operations the scheme supports, such as additions, multiplications and polynomial approximations of other functions. Exact schemes return the same answer as the unencrypted computation, while approximate schemes, often used for neural networks, return a close one. The guarantee is confidentiality of the data while it is processed, on the usual assumption that the server follows the protocol.

name: Algorithm Review Boards
description: An algorithm review board, also called an AI ethics board or AI review board, is a standing group from different disciplines that examines proposed AI systems or AI research projects before they proceed. It differs from an Institutional Review Board (IRB), which protects the human subjects of research, because it also weighs harms to the people a system will affect and to society. Many boards first sort projects by risk, and for higher-risk work the project team submits a written account of the system's purpose, data, foreseeable harms and planned mitigations, which members with technical, legal, ethical and domain backgrounds question and iterate on with the team. Where it has the power to decide, the board approves, approves with conditions such as a monitoring plan or a re-review date, or rejects; where it only advises, it recommends one of these. It keeps a dated record of its decision, reasons and conditions that later reviews and audits can check against what was built, and some organisations share that record with an oversight body or publish it.

name: Red Teaming
description: Red teaming is a structured exercise in which a team deliberately tries to make an AI system fail, so that weaknesses are found before real users or attackers find them. The organisers set the scope and the harms of concern, recruit people with a mix of skills (for example security testers, domain specialists and members of affected groups), and give them a way to log each attempt and judge whether it worked. Participants try manipulative prompts, awkward edge cases and requests designed to draw out harmful, insecure or discriminatory responses, combining many approaches where a test for one known weakness, such as prompt injection, covers only one. The result is a record of the failures found and how easily each was provoked, which is not a pass or fail verdict. It feeds a risk register (the list of known risks and who owns them) and fixes, and the exercise is repeated when the system changes.

name: Human-in-the-Loop Safeguards
description: Human-in-the-loop safeguards hold an AI system's output at a checkpoint until a trained person has reviewed it. Designers set the rules that send a case to review, such as low model confidence (the system's own estimate of how likely it is to be right), a high-stakes outcome or a request to appeal. Some schemes also review a random sample of routine cases to audit the rest. The reviewer approves, changes or rejects the output, and the record of each review shows how often people overrode the system. Review protects only where reviewers keep using independent judgement, so the design also has to guard against over-trust and fatigue.

name: Confidence Thresholding
description: Confidence thresholding uses a model score to decide whether a prediction should proceed automatically or receive different handling. For classification, a defined reject variant accepts the most likely class only when its estimated probability exceeds a chosen threshold and otherwise withholds the automatic decision. Thresholds can route withheld cases to specified review or fallback procedures, but those procedures require their own validation. Recording the score, threshold and resulting route makes the decision rule inspectable. The operating point trades automatic coverage against accepted errors, and an estimated score is not a guarantee that a decision is correct or safe.

name: Runtime Monitoring and Circuit Breakers
description: Runtime monitoring and circuit breakers observe a deployed AI service and restrict model calls when configured signals breach specified limits. In the closed state, requests pass through and recent failures are counted, while an open breaker rejects requests or provides a configured fallback, such as a cached answer, a simpler model, a rule-based default or referral to a person. After a waiting period, the half-open state permits a few trial calls and closes again only if they succeed. Model-related triggers can include immediately available signals such as input-drift scores (how far incoming data has moved from the training data) or low prediction confidence, since accuracy usually needs later outcome labels. Logs record state changes and triggering signals, supporting review of why the service was restricted without guaranteeing that the fallback is safe.

name: Model Cards
description: A model card is a short structured document published with a trained model, stating what the model is for and what it should not be used for. It reports how the model performs on stated evaluation data, with results broken down by group (for example age or sex) and by operating condition (for example lighting or device) where these matter. It also records the training data, the metrics chosen and why, ethical considerations and known caveats. Readers use the card to judge whether the model suits their purpose before they deploy it. The original proposal gives suggested sections rather than a fixed format, and a card is only as reliable as the evaluation behind it.

name: Datasheets for Datasets
description: A datasheet for a dataset is a short document that accompanies the dataset and answers a set of questions about it, in the way an electronic component comes with a datasheet. Gebru and colleagues group the questions into seven sections: why the dataset was made, what it contains, how it was collected, how it was cleaned and labelled, what it should and should not be used for, how it is distributed, and who maintains it. Creators read the questions before collecting data, answer them when the dataset is finished, and update the sheet when the dataset changes. People considering the dataset read it to judge whether it suits their task and what risks it carries. The questions are a prompt rather than a checklist, and a datasheet records what is known without testing it.

name: MLflow Experiment Tracking
description: MLflow Tracking is the part of the open-source MLflow platform that records each run of a machine learning training script. Developers add logging calls to their code, or switch on automatic logging for supported libraries. Each run's record holds its parameters (the settings chosen, including hyperparameters, which are fixed before training), its metrics (results such as accuracy), the code version, its start and end times, and output files called artefacts, such as the trained model. Runs are grouped into experiments that can be searched and compared in a web interface, and they stay on the developer's machine unless a shared tracking server is set up. The result is a dated record of how each model was built, which a reviewer can use to see what was tried and which run produced the deployed model, but only for what was actually logged.

name: Data Version Control
description: Data Version Control (DVC) is an open-source tool that records which version of a dataset or model was used at each point in a machine learning project. It works alongside Git, the standard system for tracking changes to code. DVC keeps large data and model files in separate storage, such as a cloud storage service, and puts a small pointer file into Git that holds a fingerprint (hash) of the file's contents. A team can also describe a pipeline, meaning the ordered steps from raw data through preprocessing to a trained model, and DVC then records fingerprints of each step's inputs, settings and outputs. Committed to Git, these files give a dated history of how data and models changed and let the team restore an earlier version, but only for what was added to DVC and committed.

name: Adversarial Training Evaluation
description: Adversarial training evaluation tests whether a model trained on adversarial examples (inputs altered slightly to cause errors) is really more robust, or has only learned to resist the attacks used in training. The evaluator first states a threat model, meaning the kind and size of change allowed and what the attacker knows. The model is then attacked with a varied set of strong methods, including ones not used in training, ones adapted to this particular defence, and ones that do not rely on the model's gradients, which exposes models that merely hide them. The main output is robust accuracy, the share of inputs still classified correctly under attack, plotted against the allowed size of the change and reported next to accuracy on unaltered inputs. Because attacks can only find weaknesses, the result is an upper bound on robustness, not a guarantee.

name: API Usage Pattern Monitoring
description: API usage pattern monitoring examines how each account uses a deployed model's API, to catch misuse that no single request reveals. The monitor keeps a running record per account and compares it with a baseline of normal use, raising an alert when the account departs from it. Published detectors for model theft show two ways to do this: one tests whether the distances between an account's successive queries follow the bell-shaped pattern that ordinary use produces, and another estimates how much of the model's behaviour the account's queries and responses would let someone rebuild. Providers also score how often an account triggers content filters or repeats jailbreak attempts, and send high scores for review. The output is a log of alerts and the actions taken, which gives a dated record of how the API was used compared with the uses it was approved for.

name: Data Poisoning Detection
description: Data poisoning detection looks for training examples that an attacker has planted to change how a model behaves. The best-studied case is the backdoor: a few examples carrying a hidden trigger, such as a sticker on a stop sign, are mislabelled so that the model misclassifies any input with the trigger while it performs normally on clean data. Detection first trains a model on the untrusted data, then examines how that model represents each training example internally (its activations in the last hidden layer), one class at a time. Activation clustering splits a class into two groups by those activations and flags the smaller group when the split is clear, and spectral signatures score each example by its position along the main direction of variation and flag the highest scores. The flagged examples are reviewed or removed and the model is retrained, which yields a list of suspected examples and a measure of how cleanly each class separates.

name: Jailbreak Resistance Testing
description: Jailbreak resistance testing checks whether a language model or chatbot can be talked out of its safety rules. Testers write or collect prompts that try to elicit content the system is meant to refuse, such as role-playing a character without restrictions, framing the request as hypothetical, hiding it in an encoding such as Base64, or combining several of these. Each response is judged as a refusal, a breach or unclear, by a reviewer or an automated check. The result is the rate at which each attack family succeeds, with the example prompts that worked. This shows where the safeguards fail, but only for the attacks tried.

name: Model Extraction Defence Testing
description: Model extraction defence testing checks whether a model offered through a query interface, such as a prediction API, can be copied by someone who can only send it inputs and read its outputs. The tester plays the attacker, spends a fixed query budget on the protected interface, then uses the answers to train a surrogate model (a copy trained on the answers) or to solve for the model's parameters, and compares the copy with the original. Fidelity is usually measured as the share of inputs on which the copy agrees with the original, together with how many queries that took. The same attack is run with and without each defence, such as limiting queries, rounding or removing confidence scores, or adding noise to outputs, to show how much each defence raises the attacker's cost. The tester also measures the effect on legitimate users, for example accuracy or response time.

name: Membership Inference Attack Testing
description: Membership inference attack testing checks whether someone with access to a trained model can tell if a particular record was in its training data. The tester plays the attacker, using the model's confidence scores, its prediction patterns or its loss on a record, often with shadow models, which are copies trained on similar data whose members are known. The attack is scored on records known to be members and records known to be non-members, which the tester must keep apart. The key result is the share of true members the attack identifies when it wrongly flags only a tiny share of non-members (for example 0.1%), because overall accuracy can hide an attack that identifies a few records with near certainty. The results guide the choice of mitigations, such as differential privacy or regularisation.

name: Trigger-Set Model Watermarking
description: Trigger-set model watermarking lets the owner of a trained classifier show later that a suspect model was copied from theirs, by planting a secret behaviour that only the owner can demonstrate. Before release, the owner chooses a small secret trigger set (in the originating scheme, 100 abstract images), gives each input an arbitrary label unrelated to its content, and trains or fine-tunes the model to return those labels while keeping its accuracy on the real task. In the originating scheme the owner also records cryptographic commitments to the trigger inputs and their labels, which fix the watermark at release so that a trigger set cannot be invented once a dispute has begun. To verify, the owner, or an arbiter shown the opened commitments, sends the trigger inputs to the suspect model through its ordinary prediction interface and counts how many return the assigned labels; an independently trained model matches them at about chance level, so a match rate above a preset threshold is evidence of copying. The technique produces the watermarked model, the commitments and, for each verification, the suspect model's trigger-set accuracy against the threshold.

name: Prompt Injection Testing
description: Prompt injection testing checks whether an AI system can be made to follow instructions its builders did not intend. In a direct attack the user types the instructions. In an indirect attack they are hidden in content the system reads, such as a web page, an email or a retrieved document. Testers run a library of attack patterns, such as telling the system to ignore its earlier instructions or inserting text that pretends the original task is already complete, and record how often each pattern changes the system's behaviour. Some programmes also test detectors that try to spot injected text before the system acts on it, and score them by the attacks they miss and the harmless inputs they wrongly block.

name: CycloneDX Machine Learning Bill of Materials
description: A CycloneDX ML-BOM (machine-learning bill of materials) is a machine-readable inventory of what a model is made of, written in the CycloneDX standard (ECMA-424) so that tools as well as people can check it. It applies the software bill of materials, a structured list of the components in a piece of software, to models: the model is declared as a component of type machine-learning-model with its identifiers, version, supplier, licence and file hashes, together with the base models it was derived from (its pedigree), the datasets used to train and evaluate it with their source, classification and owners, the libraries it depends on, and an optional structured model card giving its task, architecture, performance metrics, intended uses and known limitations. The BOM is written at release, by hand or with a generator that reads the model's repository and metadata, checked against the CycloneDX schema, and can be signed. Consumers then query it, for example to find every deployed model that uses a dataset or library found to be compromised, or to check a supplier's declared datasets and licences before purchase. Unlike a model card or datasheet, written for people to read, or an experiment log or data version history, which stay with the team that built the model, it is a parts list in a fixed schema that travels with the model and can be matched against vulnerability records and file hashes, but it records what its author declares and verifies none of it.

name: Malicious Model-File Scanning
description: Malicious model-file scanning checks a downloaded or received model file for code that would run when the file is loaded, without loading it. Several common ways of saving (serialising) models can carry such code, above all Python's pickle format, the default for PyTorch checkpoints and the usual format for scikit-learn models, whose files can instruct the loader to import and call any Python function, so that loading an untrusted file can hand an attacker control of the machine; since version 2.6 PyTorch's own loader by default allows only a small set of known-safe functions, but some libraries switch that off to load their models. The named method is ModelScan, an open-source scanner from Protect AI, which chooses a check by file extension and reads the file as data: for pickle-based files it lists the functions the file would import and compares them with a graded list of unsafe ones, such as the os, subprocess and socket modules and Python's built-in eval and exec, and for Keras and TensorFlow files it flags Lambda layers, which hold arbitrary Python, and operations that read or write files. It reports each finding with a severity from critical to low and exits with a non-zero code when it finds any, so a pipeline can stop the file before anything loads it. The evidence is a record that no listed unsafe call was found in the files scanned; unlike data-poisoning detection it examines the saved file rather than the training data, and it shows neither that the file is safe, nor how the model behaves, nor who produced the file.

name: Model Signing
description: Model signing lets the publisher of a machine-learning model attach a cryptographic signature to the model's files, so that anyone who later loads them can check who released them and that no file has changed since. Under the Open Source Security Foundation's Model Signing (OMS) specification and its reference tool, model-signing, the publisher computes a hash (a short fingerprint that changes if a single byte of the file changes) of every file in the model directory, such as weights, configuration, tokeniser and any dataset files kept with them, lists the hashes in a sorted manifest and signs the manifest, producing a detached signature file kept beside the model. The signature can be made with the publisher's own key, with a certificate from an organisation's certificate authority, or through Sigstore, which issues a short-lived certificate tied to a verified online identity, such as a person's account or a build pipeline's, and records each signing event in a transparency log, an append-only record that can be inspected afterwards. Before loading, the consumer verifies the signature against the signer it expects, recomputes every hash and rejects the model if any listed file differs or is missing or, unless that check is switched off, an unlisted file has appeared, so the evidence is a pass or fail tied to a named signer and an exact set of files. Unlike the unsigned file hashes kept by data-versioning tools, it shows who stands behind the files, and unlike a watermark, which is trained into the weights so that it survives in an altered copy, it is broken by any change; it says nothing about how the model behaves or what it was trained on.

name: AutoAttack
description: AutoAttack is a fixed suite of four automated adversarial attacks, introduced by Croce and Hein (ICML 2020), that measures how much of an image classifier's test accuracy survives small, deliberately chosen changes to its input images at inference time. The evaluator states the threat model, a norm and radius that bound the change (for example, no pixel value changed by more than 8/255 under the L-infinity norm), and the standard version then attacks each correctly classified test image in turn with APGD-CE (projected gradient descent that sets its own step size, on the cross-entropy loss), a targeted APGD on the authors' Difference of Logits Ratio loss, a targeted form of the FAB minimum-norm attack, and the Square Attack, which needs only the model's outputs and so still works when gradients are uninformative. An image counts as robust only if none of the four finds a misclassified version within the bound, and because every attack setting is fixed in advance the evaluator tunes nothing, which removes a common cause of overstated robustness: an attack too weakly tuned for the model. The output is robust accuracy, the share of test images still classified correctly under attack at the stated norm and radius, reported beside clean accuracy; published models are compared on the RobustBench leaderboard, which uses AutoAttack as its standard evaluation. Because AutoAttack is not built around any one defence, it can supply the attack step for a wider judgement of a defence, such as whether adversarial training holds up against attacks it was not trained on; unlike red teaming, it involves no human attacker or open-ended search.

name: STRIDE-AI Threat Modelling
description: STRIDE-AI is a threat-modelling method for machine-learning (ML) systems, proposed by Mauri and Damiani (2021, extended 2022), that lists, before any testing, the ways an attacker could compromise each asset of an ML pipeline and how serious each would be. It adapts Microsoft's STRIDE scheme, in which each of six threat types (spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege) breaks one security property (authenticity, integrity, non-repudiation, confidentiality, availability and authorisation), and gives each property an ML-specific definition: confidentiality, for example, means that querying a model reveals nothing beyond its inputs and outputs. The analyst surveys the assets produced across the ML life cycle, such as raw, labelled and validation data, hyperparameters, trained and deployed models and the model architecture, and with each asset's owners runs a failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA, a structured review of how a component could fail and with what effect), answering set questions about how the asset could fail, be misused or be abused. Each failure mode is mapped to the properties it would break and so to STRIDE threats, using the method's published tables of asset types, properties and known attacks; the analyst then works with developers to draw threat trees showing the conditions under which each threat could be realised, and rates each threat's priority (the worked example uses DREAD, which scores five factors from 1 to 10). name: Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law Risk and Impact Assessment
description: HUDERIA is the Council of Europe's methodology for identifying and assessing the risks an AI system poses to human rights, democracy and the rule of law, and for planning how to prevent or reduce them, from design through deployment to retirement. It is non-binding guidance that public and private organisations may use or adapt in whole or in part; it was drawn up to support risk assessment in line with the Council of Europe's Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence, and the human rights treaties its resources cite are illustrative, binding only the states that are parties to them. A multidisciplinary team first runs a context-based risk analysis (COBRA): it scopes the system's purpose, data and affected groups, works through risk factors in the system's application, design and deployment contexts, maps potential impacts on specific rights and on democratic and legal processes, gives each impact an initial rating, and triages the system, deciding whether further assessment is needed and whether the system should be built or deployed at all. Impacts are rated for severity, judged by scale (how serious the harm is), scope (how many people, which groups and for how long) and reversibility (whether those affected can be restored to their earlier position), and for probability; for systems that may pose significant risks, the team may engage affected stakeholders and then re-examines and re-rates each impact in a fuller risk and impact assessment. The output is a mitigation plan that prefers avoiding a harm to reducing, repairing or compensating for it, names who is responsible for each measure, outlines where appropriate the remedies open to affected people, and schedules repeat reviews as the system and its context change.

name: AI Incident Reporting with the OECD Common Reporting Framework
description: AI incident reporting with the OECD common reporting framework records each event in which an AI system caused harm, or could plausibly have caused it, in the common set of 29 fields the OECD published in February 2025, so that reports from different organisations, sectors and countries can be compared and pooled. The framework is meant for both mandatory and voluntary reporting and defines what a report contains, not the reporting interface or what should happen afterwards. The reporter first classifies the event using the OECD's definitions: an AI incident is an event in which the development, use or malfunction of an AI system directly or indirectly leads to harm to people's health, disruption of critical infrastructure, a violation of human rights or of laws protecting fundamental, labour or intellectual property rights, or harm to property, communities or the environment, and an AI hazard is one that could plausibly lead to such harm. Seven fields are mandatory: a title, a description, how the AI system was involved (as a direct cause, a contributing factor, a failure to act, through over-reliance or misuse, through human error, or through a failure to comply with the law), who is reporting, supporting material, the severity (hazard, serious hazard, incident, serious incident or disaster) and the type of harm. The other 22 record, where known and among other things, when and where it happened, the system and the organisations behind it, the people affected, the sector, how widely the system was deployed, whether training data, the model or several interacting systems were involved, the system's task and level of autonomy, and any action taken, giving an inspectable register of what went wrong in operation.

name: SMACTR Internal Algorithmic Audit
description: SMACTR is an internal audit procedure for AI systems, proposed by Raji and colleagues in 2020, in which an audit team inside the developing organisation but separate from the product team examines a system during development and before launch against the ethical objectives and requirements the organisation has declared for it. The audit runs in five stages, each producing set documents. In Scoping, auditors review the product requirements and the declared objectives and write an ethical review of the use case, drawing in independent domain experts and marginalised groups, and a social impact assessment; in Mapping, they map the people involved, review existing design records, interview the engineers and begin a failure modes and effects analysis (FMEA), a systematic review of the foreseeable ways the system could fail and their effects, used to rank risks for testing. In Artefact Collection, a checklist confirms that the expected development documents, such as model cards and datasheets, exist; in Testing, auditors run tests chosen from the FMEA's priorities, such as adversarial probing with tailored inputs, and rate each risk high, mid or low from its likelihood and severity in an ethical risk analysis chart; in Reflection, they set the results against the declared objectives, finalise the risk analysis and agree a remediation plan with the engineering team. The documents are kept in an algorithmic design history file, from which the auditors write a summary report that leadership can use to decide whether the system launches, changes or is abandoned.
